en: The Eye of the Perfect and Sudden Teaching (with Preface).
Composed by the Śramaṇa Faden of Siming.
Those who study the Mahāyāna, though they possess only the physical eye, are said to possess the Buddha-eye. Why is this? Because they clearly understand that their own bodies...

Regarding the Buddha-nature: although all phenomena are originally numinous and wondrous, they cannot be known except through the principles of the Perfectly Explanatory Teaching (*yuanquan jiaozhi*).
What, then, constitutes this Perfectly Explanatory Teaching? It is precisely the Buddha-eye and the Buddha-wisdom. When the Buddha-eye contemplates them, all sentient beings are entirely Buddhas;

when Buddha-wisdom illuminates them, there is nothing that is not the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). Ordinary people on the vast ground of existence, by means of faith in the teachings and revering these principles, [realize this].

One is able to use this Buddha-eye and Buddha-wisdom to illuminate all phenomena. Because the fleshly eye is itself the Buddha-eye, I shall now, based on the Perfect and Sudden Mahāyāna, set forth its essential tenets:
tracing them back to the mind-dharma, investigating their fundamental nature, and clarifying their underlying principles.

Exhausting the full extent of his mind, he speaks of the inherent nature (*xingju*); recounting the Dharma he has transmitted, he clarifies the three contemplations (*sanguan*) to manifest the True Teaching (*zhengzong*).
Through the mutual support of cultivation and nature, the Cool Pond may be reached. Thus, these ten chapters are titled "The Eye of the Perfect and Sudden School" (*yuantun zongyan*).

Although the text occasionally cites other sources, its intent returns to the Perfect [Teaching], for "school" (*zong*) signifies the essential. This refers to the fact that the core essence of the Perfect and Sudden Mahāyāna lies in the Buddha.

The eye is the Buddha-wisdom; this is now summarized and briefly titled. If one grasps this meaning, then one will know that the teachings of our Buddha throughout his entire life have a point of convergence.
Transmitted from patriarch to patriarch, the Dharma is not established in vain. Through practice and entry into the Way, one attains its essential core.

Fadeng is not clever; I have merely recounted these humble observations to offer a small aid to the vehicle of the Dharma. That birds head toward the mountains and a drop of dew enters the sea—this is what it means.

Preface to the *Eye of the Sudden and Perfect School*, composed on the fifth day of the intercalary month in the year Jiayin (1194) of the Shaoxi era at the Yongquan Pavilion of the Fuyan Hermitage. Following this:
The Eye of the School fundamentally takes the mind as its source,
investigating nature to clarify the Way and exhausting the universal discourse on the complete transmission of the three contemplations,
the orthodox teaching of cultivation and nature.
The *Zongyan lun* (Treatise on the Eye of the School) states: "Beginning at the Deer Park, continuing at Vulture Peak, and concluding at the Crane Forest, the Dharma was entrusted to Mahākāśyapa.
This clarifies that the Tathāgata’s Treasury of the True Dharma Eye was transmitted in succession to Kāśyapa, to endure forever."

This is the ultimate [teaching]. As for why it was entrusted to Kāśyapa: it was because he was an elder of great virtue who, through his ascetic practices and dhūta observances, was capable of succeeding to and flourishing [the Dharma];
furthermore, the conditions for this resided with him. However, as for the Dharma that was entrusted: where does it reside? How was it entrusted?
What are its dimensions? Please attempt to explain this. Some say: at the assembly on Vulture Peak, the World-Honored One held up a flower, and Kāśyapa...

That the leaf smiled is said to be its [the robe’s] characteristic sign; however, this account is entirely without textual evidence in the Indian scriptures and appears to be a later metaphorical interpretation.
Some say that the transmission of the *Prajñāpāramitā* constitutes the entrustment of the Dharma; yet this claim also fails to reflect the actual manner of the transmission.
Furthermore, when the *Prajñāpāramitā* was bestowed, it was conferred upon Subhūti and Śāriputra, not upon Kāśyapa. Others say that while the Tathāgata was present...
As for the entrustment [of the Dharma], how could it be restricted to a single time or a single place? This explanation is far too broad and general.

Some say that when the World-Honored One entrusted his robe, he was simultaneously entrusting the Dharma. Others say that after the World-Honored One entered parinirvāṇa, Kāśyapa arrived later, and the Buddha manifested his two feet, which constituted the entrustment of the Dharma.
Observing these two accounts, they can at best serve as symbolic representations; how could they be the actual characteristics of the entrustment of the Dharma? Nevertheless...
Regarding the doctrine of the transmission of the Dharma: if its characteristics are not clearly defined, one will not know what kind of Dharma is being transmitted.
Furthermore, if one does not understand how it was bestowed and received through the successive patriarchs—being ignorant of its essential core—then even the act of transmission becomes difficult.
Under such circumstances, there would be only the name of "transmission and maintenance" without its actual substance. Alas! Even the ancients regarded hearsay and idle talk with suspicion.
They deride him; how much more so when they do not understand the reason why? Moreover, the Way of the Buddhas and Patriarchs has remained exceptionally radiant and flourishing until the present day;

could this be so without a specific reason? It is said that later generations gave rise to divergent views, leading to the doctrine of the "Separate Transmission Outside the Teachings," which is also said to consist merely in the "Plucking of the Flower.
Furthermore, although those who study the Buddha [engage with] both the teachings and Chan, the teachings...
They are not the same. Since they all rely upon the Buddha, they must take the Buddha-dharma as their standard. The Buddha-dharma is precisely that which was transmitted by Kāśyapa.
That which was transmitted by Kāśyapa does not fail to originate from the Dharma of the Deer Park, the Vulture Peak, and the final Nirvāṇa at the Śāla Grove.
When, then, could there ever have been another transmission? To investigate its origins, it appears that [the proponents of other traditions] simply do not comprehend its source.
Fearing that the teachings might become confused with Chan, there arose the doctrine of the "Separate Transmission. Yet they failed to realize that such a distinction is untenable.
For instance, when the Tathāgata appeared, he manifested the eightfold voice and the four analytical knowledges; what Kāśyapa transmitted was precisely this teaching.

This teaching clarifies the mind and penetrates the principle—how could there be any practice or realization superior to this? Some may claim it is "transmitting mind by means of mind," but this is merely a figurative expression.
I do not know for what reason you have come to believe that this mind can be transmitted. Is it perhaps because the teachings serve as its interpretation?
Furthermore, since the nature of words and letters is itself liberation, one knows that both Chan and the teachings point to that which was entrusted by the Buddha on Vulture Peak to Kāśyapa.
How could one then turn their back on the Buddhas and Patriarchs? If you do not accept what was transmitted by Kāśyapa, why even speak of succeeding to the lineage?

It is thus. Those who act in this manner do so because they do not know the essential point of what is being transmitted. Now, the transmission of the Dharma is the transmission of the Buddha’s essential heart-mind.
One should know that this essential point has both general and specific aspects. Specifically, it refers to all the teachings spoken throughout the course of his entire life.
The *Prajñāpāramitā* explains its characteristics in full detail; yet within the *Prajñā*, although the two vehicles have understood it, they have not received it.
In summary, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* opens up the provisional and reveals the real, teaching the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*buddhajñānadarśana*) and pointing out the source of all phenomena.
Everything previously taught was nothing other than skillful means; now the reality is revealed as being entirely the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. Although [the first week]...
It is said that Kāśyapa had not yet understood; therefore, [the Buddha] used the parable of the high, wide, and great chariot to explain it to him.
Upon hearing this, Kāśyapa leaped for joy and received it with full understanding. This was because the Buddha’s knowledge and vision encompass all knowledge and vision;

thus, it is said that the Unsurpassed True Dharma was entrusted to Kāśyapa. In the *Śraddhādhimukti-parivarta*, the essential points are fully grasped. Thus, one knows that the transmission of the Dharma—
The Master was at Mount Ling; he had nothing else to say, but merely pointed out the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
Although the Dharma pervades both the Great and Small Vehicles, here all returns to the One Path. As the Sūtra says: "What I now possess is all that you possess;
I entrust this family inheritance to you. The impoverished son rejoiced. Jingxi said: "Knowledge and vision are both what is possessed; therefore, the Dharma..."
The flower was merely described in general terms as the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. The ancients said, "The World-Honored One held up the flower; Kāśyapa smiled. Is this not an analogy for this?
This Buddha-knowledge and vision—what person does not possess it? What dharma is not thus? It was entrusted at Vulture Peak simply for this purpose.
From patriarch to patriarch it has been transmitted; what is transmitted is this Dharma. When the Great Master Zhiyi attained awakening, he awakened to this.

It is the Dharma. Even if one possesses the eloquence of a cascading river, it is this Dharma that one would expound. Nāgārjuna employed written words to broaden the understanding of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*);
he broadened this Dharma. The inconceivable *Mahā-śamatha-vipaśyanā* (Great Calming and Contemplation), with its three contemplations within a single mind, illuminates this Dharma.

Riding this precious vehicle, one proceeds directly to the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) to realize this Dharma. The single transmission of the mind-seal by Bodhidharma was the transmission of this very Dharma.
How magnificent is this Dharma! It is the source and root of both Chan and the Teachings. Though their streams differ, their source must be the same.
As for their ultimate destination, it is simply one and the same. If one pursues the current while losing the source, then one will not know the essential point of what has been transmitted.
To do so would be to辜负 (betray) the Tathāgata’s appearance in the world; the way of transmission and reception would thus vanish at this point.
If one relies upon this Dharma, every dharma is fully manifest as originally perfected and present. Thus, the Buddhas and Patriarchs...
Before they appeared, not even a hair’s breadth was lacking; though Buddhas and patriarchs have appeared, not a single thread of hair has been added.
Dīpaṃkara had no dharma to give to Śākyamuni, and Śākyamuni likewise had no dharma to speak. Therefore it is said: "If one says that the Tathāgata has preached any dharma, one slanders the Buddha.
Yet this is not the same as the Buddhas and patriarchs; how can this Way be known? If one knows this, then the Buddhas and patriarchs—
There is nothing further to be transmitted. Nevertheless, "Though the Buddha-dharma exists, if no one speaks it, though one possesses wisdom, one cannot realize it.
If the Dharma were not transmitted to deliver sentient beings, there would ultimately be no way to repay their kindness; thus, the Way that is transmitted must not remain obscure.
Yuanxin of Piling said: "To remain unchanging while following conditions is called nature (*xing*); to follow conditions while remaining unchanging is called mind (*xin*).

Thus, one knows that although mind and nature are identical in essence, they are distinct in meaning. That which makes them identical is that non-change is itself the following of conditions, and the following of conditions is itself non-change.
This is because it is unchanging. As for why there are differences: although the nature of all phenomena is equal, Buddhas and sentient beings arise according to defiled or pure conditions.
By virtue of pure conditions, one accords with the fundamental nature and manifests the true mind, thereby becoming a Buddha.
Due to the conditions of defilement, one becomes deluded regarding its original nature and gives rise to false thoughts; thus there are sentient beings.

Therefore, we know that the minds of sentient beings possess both the real and the false. The false arises by following the conditions of defilement, whereas the real is the unchanging nature that remains entirely unchanged.
Because it follows conditions, the entire true mind becomes false thought; hence it is said: "The entirety of the real creates the false," and within the false, the real is fully present.
The three thousand [realms]—when one penetrates this deluded mind, not a single sign of identity or difference exists, yet the three thousand remain vividly present.

This is because although its substance is fundamentally true, it is manifested through deluded thought. Thus, Siming said: "It refers to the 'infinitesimal' mind as the essential point for understanding phenomena and principle, and for practice.

How profound is this intent! Therefore, to recognize the true mind, one must take deluded thought as its very substance; without grasping this principle, one will not know how to give rise to awakening.
Regarding the locus of contemplation, if one fails to penetrate the gateway that reveals the sublime, the source of the school’s doctrine will fall into disorder.

The *Jiuxing lun* (Treatise on Investigating Nature) states: "In the equal and true dharma-realm, the Buddha does not deliver sentient beings. It further states: "Within the realm of True Suchness, birth and death are utterly severed."
The Buddha’s provisional designation [of "nature"] is that within the state of equality there is no form of self or other;
these all refer to its fundamental nature. All people speak of this nature, yet there is a slight difference between them.

Zhongni (Confucius) spoke only of the "Mandate of Heaven," which refers to the spontaneity of nature without declaring it to be either good or evil. As for Xunzi, he stated that "nature is exclusively evil."
Mencius said that human nature is exclusively good. Yangzi, however, said that its nature is a mixture of good and evil.

Now, those who exhaustively define nature in terms of good and evil have not yet reached the essence of nature; they have merely grasped the manifestations (*qing*) of nature, not its fundamental substance (*ti*).
Now, joy, anger, sorrow, fear, love, hate, and desire—these are called the seven emotions (*qí qíng*). All of these are expressions of good and evil. Nature itself is not [merely] these...
This which I teach as its nature is neither good nor evil, neither delusion nor awakening, neither cause nor effect, and neither internal nor external.
It is equal to empty space, pervading the Dharma-realm without distinction of high or low, and transcending the marks of self and other.
Since it is neither delusion nor awakening, nor cause nor effect, it is called "equality. One should know that this nature is the principle within phenomena;

causes and effects, ordinary beings and sages, self and others—all are phenomena within that principle. Since this principle is itself the principle, it is devoid of any distinction between high and low;
therefore, it is said that "this dharma is equal. Although this principle manifests as good and evil, causes and effects, it is nonetheless endowed with goodness.
Regarding evil causes and effects, one should know that the minds of sentient beings are precisely this nature; therefore, it is able to universally encompass all phenomena.

This is because this nature is the principle of the true mark of *tathatā*. This nature possesses two meanings: first, the meaning of immutability; second, the meaning of not abiding in its own nature.
The meaning of not abiding in its own nature is precisely "following conditions" (*suiyuan*). Although it is said to follow...
Because its substance does not change, it is said that "not changing" constitutes its meaning.
It is clear that within the Way there are those who take substance as the Way and those who take function as the Way. Substance is precisely the substance of function; function is...
This is precisely the function of the substance itself; thus, one knows that substance and function cannot be separated. As the ancients said: "What Heaven mandates is called nature (xing);
following nature is called the Way (dao); cultivating the Way is called instruction (jiao). This Way is that which must not be left for even a moment."
One may thus depart from what is not the Way. This shows that the Way exists by virtue of nature; through the Way, one realizes nature.
Since the Way has "penetration" as its essential meaning, it is able to lead one toward nature. Since nature is all-pervasive, treading upon it constitutes the Way.
Since the Way is identical to nature, pointing to nature is itself pointing to the Way. Therefore, nature and the Way are neither one nor different. Because they are not one...
The Way exists by virtue of its nature (*xing*), for it is not distinct from it; thus, one takes this very nature as the Way of humanity. Therefore it is said:
"The Master’s Way is simply *zhong* (sincerity) and *shu* (reciprocity). *Zhong* means to exhaust the mind; *shu* means to measure others by the standard of oneself.
Exhausting the mind is precisely nature; measuring others by the standard of oneself is precisely following nature. Since both are called the Way of the Master, we know that...

The Way possesses both essence and function. As for those in the Buddhist teachings who clarify the Way, it is as they say: "The Bhagavāns of the ten directions have but one path to the gate of Nirvāṇa";
"All unhindered people take this one path to transcend birth and death. That the Way is singular is because of the single nature;
thus, nature itself is the Way, and it is therefore called the "One Path. Since it is said that there is a "transcending," this takes function as its basis.
The Way is precisely the function of the essence itself. If one says that there are not two ways in the world, this is what Buddhism terms the "Unsurpassed Way" (*anuttara-mārga*).
It is called "unsurpassed" because it is identical with the nature (*dharmatā*). This, however, is not a nature characterized by delusion or enlightenment.

Nevertheless, the Confucian and Buddhist clarifications of the Way each differ in their scope, being respectively small and great. As for the Confucian school, they take Yao and Shun as their model...

The Great Way. For the Three Kings, it was the Small Way. In Buddhism, the four periods and three teachings are considered the Small Way, while the *Lotus Sūtra*’s revelation of the provisional as the ultimate constitutes the Great Way.
That which is attained as the Great Way is so because it accords with one’s nature;

thus it is said that the natures of Yao and Shun emerged from benevolence (*ren*) and righteousness (*yi*), yet these arose merely through following their nature and diligent practice, rather than through a path of benevolence and righteousness itself. This is likely because they had not heard of Buddhism.
Clarifying the Way: it does not go beyond Great Compassion (*mahāmaitrī*). When this compassion accords with the nature of reality (*dharmatā*), it is called "unconditioned" (*nirālamba*).

Therefore, it is said: "If compassion were to have an end, it would not be unconditioned compassion. Since compassion is inexhaustible, it is entirely due to its accordance with the nature. This unconditioned compassion is none other than the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*);

it is named the Great Way (*mahāmārga*). Thus, it is said: "The power of the roots of goodness of compassion functions spontaneously; it is neither a matter of deliberate mental effort (*manasikāra*) nor..."
It is not something cultivated separately; therefore, it is called "unconditioned" (*anabhisaṃskāra*). When the initial mind gives rise to this, it is named the "Unsurpassed Way.

When the fruit of the mind is fully realized, this too is called "unsurpassed. As previously stated, that the Way possesses both essence and function does not go beyond what is meant by cultivation and nature.
This serves as the thread that runs through all of it. Indeed, there is nothing that surpasses this when the sages speak their teachings to clarify the Way.

Qiong Bian of Biling said: "Since one has already believed that this nature exists within one's own mind, he next demonstrates that this nature is neither internal nor external, but pervades all of space."
The emptiness of the mind is identical to that of all Buddhas, equal to space. Thus one knows that the essential nature of the sentient being’s mind is all-pervasive.
Therefore, the treatise says: "The essence of the mind is free from thought; as for this state of being free from thought, it is equal to the realm of space and there is nowhere it does not pervade.
Consequently, the mind of sentient beings is the very body of the great awakening, perfect and eternal. This body is Vairocana, pervading all places.
There is not a single dharma that is not my own mind. Therefore it is said: "When the mind roams through the Dharma-realm as if it were empty space, one then knows the realm of all Buddhas.
One should know that this mind is vast and boundless, reaching everywhere. Because from time immemorial we have failed to realize that the mind is omnipresent, it is said:
"I am confined to Vairocana, except for the physical aggregates. Internally, one must know that [the mind] pervades the ten directions.
Empty space is not separate from my mind. Thus, the Sūtra says: "Space arises within the Great Enlightenment, like a single bubble emerging from the ocean.
If one does not recognize that the mind is all-pervasive, then the full meaning [of this analogy] cannot be revealed. Not only is this mind omnipresent;

one should know that all dharmas are likewise so. Therefore it is said: "Even if a student knows that the internal mind contains the three thousand dharmas, if they do not know that my mind is pervasive, [they have not truly understood]."
The same applies to each of those trichiliocosms, which mutually pervade one another. One should understand that the essence of reality is fundamentally devoid of the four natures;

thus, mind, Buddha, and sentient beings are non-differentiated in the threefold sense. Therefore, by raising a single instance, the whole is entirely encompassed; these various realms enter into one another without any obstruction.
Since it has been discussed that the mind of sentient beings already pervades all things, one knows that all dharmas are fundamentally inherent within the mind. Therefore, it is said:

"The environment and inhabitants of Avīci hell are entirely contained within the self-mind of the Ultimate Sage; the body and land of Vairocana do not exceed the state of the lowliest ordinary person."

A single thought-moment. Furthermore, a sutra states: "If one does not know that the physical body, extending outward to the mountains, rivers, and empty space, are all things within the wondrously luminous true body, then one fails to realize that the ten realms, the thousand suchnesses, and the three thousand worlds are fully present in a single thought-moment;
there is nothing that is not simply the mind alone. Thus, all dharmas are mutually complete within one another. Therefore, Siming said: "Of the myriad phenomena..."
Since it is already granted that form is possessed by the mind, why should it not be granted that the mind possesses the thousandfold differences of form?

Why is this so? Because all phenomena are the Dharma-realm; therefore, they are able to fully possess all phenomena. The reason each and every thing is adorned and thus complete is precisely because of their pervasiveness.
One should know that all phenomena and the single mind are fundamentally no different from one another; phenomena are themselves [the mind].

The mind—this very mind is the Dharma. For the purpose of pointing it out, it is said that the mind is inherently complete, without any distinction between a subject that possesses and an object that is possessed.
One should know that the ten directions and the three periods of time do not depart from the tip of a single hair; how could the lands and their atoms transcend a single thought-moment?

Therefore, the Sutra says: "The body and mind are perfectly luminous and unmoving within the site of enlightenment; upon the tip of a single hair, they can universally contain the lands of the ten directions.

Thus we know that the dharma of the three thousand worlds is fully present in a single thought-moment. The three thousand are identical to the one thought-moment, and the one thought-moment is identical to the three thousand.
This is not due to their mutual production, nor is it due to their mutual containment. It is like the eight characteristics of a thing, or the eight virtues of water.

This can be understood through analogy. Since it is thus that the mind is inherently endowed [with all phenomena], so too is its transformation. If one raises a single thought-moment, the Buddhas and sentient beings, along with their environments and bodies, appear in their distinct clarity.

Therefore, know that within a single thought-moment and a single mind, both phenomena and principle are fully present. It is because they are fundamentally endowed according to principle that their phenomenal functions arise;
this meaning may now be understood.
The Buddha’s single transformation as transmitted from above to below is such that, to state the essentials of the Dharma he transmitted, it does not go beyond the three contemplations.
This Dharma of the three contemplations— the inconceivable realm— is precisely the profound realm of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, pointed out for the sake of sentient beings by the Buddha.
This Buddha-knowledge and vision does not transcend the full realm of the Three Truths. To give rise to wisdom and reflect back upon this realm is precisely what is called the Three Contemplations;
this is the wondrous understanding and wondrous practice transmitted within our school, entrusted at Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa and inherited by Kāśyapa.
The successive patriarchs have transmitted [the Dharma] from one to another, and nothing has emerged outside of this.

Thus, the *Mohe zhiguan* (Great Calming and Contemplation) traces the source by following its currents, beginning with the Greatly Awakened World-Honored One’s proclamation of this Way, down to the present master who received it from Nāgārjuna; there is nothing that is not this Way of the Three Contemplations.
The essence of this Way is the wondrous principle of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), and this principle is precisely the fundamental mind of sentient beings and all phenomena.

As for its essential nature: that which can illuminate this principle is called "contemplation" (vipaśyanā). When contemplation is perfected and the principle is revealed, it returns to this very nature.
Although the Chan school does not explicitly clarify the three contemplations, it nonetheless does not fall outside of them. As they say: "Directly pointing at the human mind."

"Seeing one's nature is attaining Buddhahood. This direct pointing is not a subtle understanding; seeing one's nature is not a subtle practice; and attaining Buddhahood is not a returning to the source?
However, because ordinary beings on this vast ground are muddled, distracted, and restless, they must cultivate *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.

Moreover, for those of superior capacity whose very nature is such that "the mind itself is Buddha," there is no need for deliberation; how could they remain stuck in objective states or meditative observations? [The questioner] says: "If one already knows that the mind itself is..."
The Buddha—how could he be apart from the stream of understanding and practice? If there were not wondrous understanding, how could one know that the mind is suchness?

If there were not wondrous practice, how could one realize that the mind is suchness? One should know that from those below the Buddha down, practitioners do not depart from the path of the three contemplations.
Thus, Jingxi said: "Even if a sage from India were to come in person, it would not equal the descent of the two births in Tuṣita. Therefore...
The Great Being of Dongyang (Dongyang Dashi) occupies the stage of Equal Enlightenment (Samyaksambodhi), yet he still takes the three contemplations and four movements as the essence of his practice.

It even states: "Furthermore, the three contemplations... This is the oral transmission from the lips of the Great Being of the *Yingluo* (Adornment) Sutra, who is a candidate for Buddhahood within our own school.

Thus, we know that the teachings of this single lineage (the Tiantai school) are distantly derived from the Buddha’s scriptures; furthermore, they accord with the Great Being like two halves of a tally. Therefore, we know that the Way of the Three Contemplations...
It is not that this is merely what was practiced at the beginning. Zhizhe’s own statement that the dharma-gate he himself practiced was precisely this dharma is what Zhanran refers to.
However, if one relies on what was transmitted by Kāśyapa—the dharma of an entire era from the Bodhi tree to the Śāla grove—how could it consist of the three contemplations alone?
To raise such a doubt is to fail to understand the scope of the three contemplations.

Why is this so? Although the Dharma-gates taught by the Tathāgata upon his appearance in the world are immeasurable, when he reached Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa to reveal their ultimate meaning, they all converged in the Buddha Vehicle (*buddhayāna*).
This Buddha Vehicle is precisely the Three Truths (*trisatya*).

Since it is pointed out that all immeasurable Dharma-gates are identical with the Three Truths, we know that the principle of these Three Truths fully encompasses all phenomena. Furthermore, since the Three Contemplations (*trivipaśyanā*) are identical with the Three Truths...

Established. This contemplative method (guanfa) embodies immeasurable dharmas. Therefore, Jingxi said: "Thus, the Ten Profundities (shimiao) are extracted as the great essence of the contemplative method.
Furthermore, since these Ten Profundities encompass all immeasurable dharma-gates, these dharma-gates do not transcend the Three Thousand [Worlds].
This very three thousandfold world-system constitutes the substance of the three contemplations (*trividha-vipaśyanā*). Thus, it reveals that the three contemplations encompass immeasurable dharmas.

Therefore, it is said that "cessation and contemplation (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*) subsume all teachings and all practices," thereby manifesting that the substance of the three contemplations is vast and complete, fully endowed both horizontally and vertically.
Why is this so? It is because among all phenomena, every dharma is mutually inclusive, even extending to the minds of sentient beings.
It is likewise so. Since the three thousand realms already abide within a single thought-moment, this is precisely the Buddha-nature of the three contemplations (*trividha-vipaśyanā*).

Because these three contemplations arise from this Buddha-nature, this contemplation encompasses all phenomena without exception. Thus, one knows that the three contemplations and all phenomena do not follow divergent paths.

If one does not clarify this, then to merely speak of "transmitting and upholding" [the Dharma] is in vain; for although the Chan school does not esteem conceptual discrimination, [it must still rely on this principle].

It is simply said that there is "direct transmission pointing directly," yet this essentially does not depart from this Way. If one were to say otherwise, Śākyamuni would have had two minds, and Kāśyapa would have split into two lineages.
If you wish to understand this meaning and seek the source of the school, it is impossible to fathom its depth by following the branches and drifting with the current.
Regarding the Three Contemplations, Jingxi said: "A single thought-moment devoid of marks is called emptiness; that no dharma is not fully contained within it is called the provisional;
that it is neither identical nor different is called the Middle. Self-benefit and benefiting others are exhausted in this alone. This was the teaching with which the Master [Zhiyi] faced his death.
The Way of the Three Contemplations is shown to future generations as the essential core of the mind. As for these Three Contemplations: the Wise One (Zhiyi) received them from Mount Nanyue;
Mount Nanyue transmitted them to the Northern Qi; and the Northern Qi inherited them from Nāgārjuna. Therefore it is said:
Master Wen follows the *Śāstra* (the *Dazhidu lun*) in his application of mind entirely. If one investigates its ultimate source, it is evident that it does not originate solely with Nāgārjuna.
Thus, the *Yili* states: "Furthermore, the three contemplations (*san guan*) are fundamentally based on the *Ratnakūṭa-sūtra* (the *Yingluo jing*).

Since they were personally received from the golden mouth of the Bodhisattva who is next to attain Buddhahood, we know with certainty that they originally derive from the Greatly Awakened World-Honored One himself. Nevertheless, regarding the source of these three contemplations, some say they originate from the *Yingluo*.
Some call it the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, some the *Jñāna-śāstra*, and some the *Madhyamaka-śāstra*. To which one specifically does this refer? It is said:

The method of the Three Contemplations has its textual source in the *Ratnakūṭa* and the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, yet its essential meaning culminates in the Perfect and Sudden teaching of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
It was transmitted by the various patriarchs, praised by Nāgārjuna, and expanded upon by Tiantai. Thus, the *Sishinianchu* states: "If one discusses the numerical completeness..."

The feet must rely upon the *Avataṃsaka* (Necklace). If one relies on the sequence of the three contemplations (*trivipaśyanā*), one must rely on the *Mahāvaipulya-mahāsannipāta-avadāna-sūtra* (Great Vaipulya Necklace Sutra).

The sutra says: "Entering emptiness from the conventional is the contemplation of the two truths; entering the conventional from emptiness is the contemplation of equality. These two contemplations serve as the skillful means to enter the Middle Way, the contemplation of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
That which emerges from the *Mahāvaipulya* is stated in the sutra: "Desiring to be fully endowed with the wisdom of the Path..."

One who desires the wisdom of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*) should study the *prajñāpāramitā*. One who desires to fulfill all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*) by means of the wisdom of the aspects of the path should study the *prajñāpāramitā*.
One who desires to fulfill the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*) by means of all-knowledge should study the *prajñāpāramitā*.

One who desires to sever the afflictions (*kleśa*) along with their residual tendencies (*vāsanā*) by means of the knowledge of all modes should study the *prajñāpāramitā*. One who desires [the wisdom of] the path (*mārgajñatā*) [and] the emptiness [of the path], and one who desires the wisdom of the aspects of the path...
"Wisdom" (provisionally) refers to the desire to fulfill all aspects through all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*) [the middle];

"all-aspect knowledge" (*sarvākārajñatā*) refers to the desire to sever afflictions along with their residual habits [the wisdom of the exhaustion of delusions] [the ultimate]. According to these two sūtras, both clarify the three contemplations; therefore, it is called the *Adornment of the Original School* (*Mūla-yukti-alaṃkāra*).
It is further stated: "The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (Dapin) is taken as the method of contemplation (*guanfa*), yet its ultimate purport (*yizhi*) converges upon the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.

This is because the Perfect and Sudden [teaching]—by means of opening up the provisional to reveal the real—unifies all teachings such that there is nothing that is not the single mind and the threefold contemplation. Thus says the *Yili*:

To take the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* as the core essence—this is precisely what is meant by that. As for its transmission to the various patriarchs, it is this very path transmitted from Kāśyapa onwards.

Regarding the praise attributed to Nāgārjuna: since the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* contains the textual passage on the "three wisdoms," and the scripture’s phrasing appears to follow the sequence of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, he took the underlying intent of this text and spoke of the three wisdoms; yet these truly exist [within the sūtra].
The three wisdoms are attained within a single mind. Since they reside in a single mind, wisdom is accomplished through contemplation (*guan*).

If there were not the three contemplations within a single mind, how could the three wisdoms within a single mind be accomplished? Therefore, since wisdom already exists, one reveals contemplation through wisdom; thus, one also perceives the three contemplations within a single mind.
To take the *Zhonglun* (Mūlamadhyamakakārikā) as a guide—does it not lie herein? However, the *Zhonglun* directly elucidates the three contemplations without...

It speaks of the "one mind. Therefore it says: "Of those dharmas produced by causes and conditions, I say they are empty; they are also called provisional names, and they are also called the meaning of the Middle Way.
Although this passage extends its application to various teachings, its primary meaning correctly returns to the Perfect [Teaching]. Why?

Because it states that they are "identical to emptiness," yet also states that they are "called provisional names" and so forth; this reveals that within a single dharma there are precisely these three aspects. Is this not so?

Is this not the meaning of "round" (*yuan*)? However, because it does not explicitly state that the one mind is [the essence], it further employs the passage concerning the three wisdoms being truly one mind to clarify that the three contemplations are likewise one mind.
Thus, it is known that its significance is clear when praised alongside Nāgārjuna’s works.

Since these sections are common to the various teachings of the patriarchs, there is no hindrance to interpreting their meaning according to the specific text; hence it is said: "If the four propositions are paired..."

The teaching is a distinct tradition from its own time. Some may raise a doubt, asking: "I do not yet know exactly upon which text the Northern Qi school relied—was it the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (Chizhi lun) or the *Mūlamadhyamaka-kārikā* (Zhong lun)?
If you say it was the *Madhyamaka*, why does the *Zhi guan* state that Master Wen’s application of mind followed the *Vyākhyāyukti* (Shi lun) exclusively?
If you say it was the *Vyākhyāyukti*, then our own school precisely takes the *Mūlamadhyamaka* as its fundamental method of contemplation; how could this be the *Vyākhyāyukti*?"

Is this not a treatise? Now, it is said that the Northern Qi school followed the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* for its fourfold contemplation of dharmas, and further utilized the passage from the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* concerning the three kinds of wisdom being truly one in mind to clarify and establish the "one mind and three contemplations.

Zhiyi, Guanxin, and Jingxi merely state that the *Śāstra on Wisdom* (the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*) is so called because it was extracted in brief from within the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā*; therefore, they refer to it collectively as the *Śāstra on Wisdom*.

[They are] equal. The *Fuxing* (Supplementary Practice) says: "The Dharma was entrusted [to him]. The *Chuan* (Biography) says: "Nāgārjuna composed the *Mahā-vaiśāradya-śāstra* in one hundred thousand verses;

the *Mūlamadhyamaka-kārikā* is a brief extraction of its general outline, consisting of five hundred verses. That which is now in the Tripiṭaka, annotated by Qingmu (*Candrakīrti*), is this very work.

A doubt arises: At the assembly on Vulture Peak, the Dharma was entrusted to Kāśyapa. Since the *Mūlamadhyamaka* contemplates phenomena (*dharmas*), it should belong to the Prajñāpāramitā; how can it be exhaustive?
It was transmitted to Nāgārjuna. If this is so, then was what was transmitted from Kāśyapa down to before Nāgārjuna not the three contemplations?
It is said: Although the *Prajñāpāramitā* was entrusted [to him], he did not yet receive it; it was only upon reaching the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* that he was able to believe and understand it.
Although the *Prajñāpāramitā* had been preached, it had not yet been fully elucidated; it was only upon reaching Nāgārjuna that it was praised and expounded. After Nāgārjuna passed away...

The masters of doctrinal classification do not intend to clarify the text of the *Prajñāpāramitā* by means of the meaning of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. Rather, they elucidate the three contemplations within one mind.

One should know that for those with sharp faculties on Vulture Peak, detailed explanation was unnecessary; this is, for example, like the two types of emptiness—of nature and of characteristics—which the sutra mentions with only a single phrase.
The four phrases were opened up for the sake of those with dull faculties. Therefore, it is said that the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* merely contemplates phenomena.
This refers to those of dull faculties in the final age. Although the circumstances and conditions were not explained in detail at Vulture Peak, it does not prevent one from attaining realization;
for what was previously taught has been passed down through successive patriarchs as a model since after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa. Thus, it is said that "it was transmitted to the various patriarchs.
If we rely on the assembly at Vulture Peak, however, it was only the Buddha’s knowledge and vision that Kāśyapa transmitted. Why?
Is it because they possess the meaning of the three contemplations? It is said: The Buddha’s knowledge and vision are nothing other than the Buddha-nature of the three truths.
Since he uses this Dharma to point it out to sentient beings, those who wish to enter this path must do so through contemplative observation. It is by means of such observation that they perceive it.

This is precisely what is called the Three Contemplations (*trivipaśyanā*). Thus, one knows that although the Vulture Peak (*Gṛdhrakūṭa*) did not explain this in detail, its meaning was nonetheless complete there.

Therefore, while Kāśyapa transmitted it to the various patriarchs, it was Nāgārjuna who explained it in detail through his commentaries on the sūtras. It is not that the patriarchs prior to him failed to transmit this path.
As for the statement that it was expanded upon at Tiantai, there is nothing in the *Mohe zhiguan* (*Mahā-śamatha-vipaśyanā*) that does not extensively clarify these three.
This is the method of contemplation. An objection is raised: "The three contemplations (*trividha-vipaśyanā*) of the *Yingluo* [Sūtra] appear to follow a sequential order.

Why, then, does your school take this sequential method as its transmitted teaching? The response is: "The Dharma of Perfect and Sudden Enlightenment has no separate essence; it takes the sequential itself to be the non-sequential.
Moreover, following the sequential text of the *Yingluo*, there is also the 'Three Contemplations of the Dharma-realm' (*dharmadhātu-trividha-vipaśyanā*)."
Is this not the meaning of the Perfect [Teaching]? One should understand it through its underlying intent rather than being constrained by the literal text.

Since this section belongs to the Vaipulya (Vaipulya/Square-Equivalent) class, and the most honored among them is exclusively the Perfect, if we discuss it according to its excellence, it refers to the three contemplations of the Perfect.

Thus, one knows that the Way of the Three Contemplations transmitted by our school originates from the Buddha’s sutras, was handed down by the various patriarchs, was praised by Nāgārjuna, and was expanded upon by Tian-tai [Zhiyi].

[This concerns] Tiantai. A doubter asks: "If you claim that what was transmitted by Tiantai also consists of the three contemplations (*trividha-vipaśyanā*), then consider the *Mohe zhiguan* (Great Calming and Contemplation), which primarily elucidates the inconceivable realm (*acintya-viṣaya*) of contemplation.
Within the realm of cultivated virtue (*bhāvanā-guṇa-viṣaya*), it clarifies the characteristics of cultivation;

it follows the tradition of Nāgārjuna and speaks only of the contemplation of the emptiness of nature and characteristics (*svabhāva-lakṣaṇa-śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*). On what basis can we see that the three contemplations are fully present therein? [The author] says: Tian...

Regarding the three contemplations (*trividha-vipaśyanā*) taught by the Tiantai school, there is a concern that one might merely attain emptiness. Since all phenomena are empty, they remain perfectly manifest in their own place;

being neither identical nor different, they inherently possess the three contemplations. Therefore, although only emptiness is explicitly clarified within the objects of cultivated virtue (*bhāvanā-ālambana*), it nonetheless encompasses all three.

This is precisely what is intended when the *Mohe Zhiguan* concludes with the three contemplations following the discussion of the three objects. This is analogous to the three [realms] in the *Lotus Sūtra*.

Within the *Mèiyí* (Manual of Ritual Procedures), the method of contemplation (*guānfǎ*) is clarified; however, even these four lines merely clarify emptiness (*śūnyatā*), which already encompasses the three contemplations (*sānguān*).
Why is it that one sees that the three are complete? As Siming said: "The *Fǎhuá sānmèiyí* (Manual of the Lotus Samādhi) briefly clarifies the three contemplations."
There are nine kinds of signs of realization that serve as clear evidence. Thus, we know that the contemplative methods elucidated by this school do not transcend the three contemplations.
How magnificent! This path is truly the essential art for returning to one's nature and restoring the source.
Although all sentient beings possess the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, if they are not illuminated by this path, by what means could they attain awakening? However—
Those who have not grasped the essential meaning point to the study of words and letters, claiming it is not the way to exhaustively investigate principle and fully realize one's nature.
How lamentable!

The Fourth Patriarch of the True Lineage, Siming, said: "It refers to the infinitesimal mind as the essential point for understanding phenomena, principle, and the practice of realization. How magnificent! This teaching.
This fully encapsulates the great purport of the *Mohe zhiguan*. Is not the revival of the teachings and contemplation dependent upon this?

Does one not attain the Way of Tiantai profoundly through this teaching? However, if one discusses how all phenomena are mutually complete and every dharma interpenetrates, there is a specific intention behind why [the text] points exclusively to the mind;
it is merely for the sake of remedial treatment (pratipakṣa). Thus, there is an underlying intention.

The mind is the source of all phenomena and the essential gateway for entering the Path; it is easily severed from discursive thought. Therefore, by pointing out the delusion, one shows people how to return to the root and restore the source.
As for the remedies employed, the *Four Foundations of Mindfulness* states:

"Beings of the upper realms are mostly attached to the mind, so they are instructed to contemplate external forms. Beings of the lower realms are mostly attached to external forms, so they are instructed to contemplate the internal mind."
Since the sutras and treatises frequently clarify the contemplation of the mind, a doubt arises:

for what reason should one know that the essential path of this school points exclusively to a single thought-moment as the core of phenomena, principle, understanding, and practice? It is said: these are all the fundamental tenets of Tiantai.
In the beginning of the *Mohe zhiguan*, the method of contemplation for the Initial Vehicle clarifies that within a single thought-moment (ekakṣaṇa) there are the three thousand realms.

These three thousand realms consist of both phenomena (*dharma*) and principle (*li*). Therefore, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*’s teaching on "the mind creates" is cited as proof. Jingxi [Zhiyi] said: "Regarding the statement 'the mind creates,' there are two meanings:
first, in terms of principle; second, in terms of phenomena. Since it is pointed out that a single thought-moment possesses these phenomena and principles, therefore—
The Fourth Clarification (Sì míng) grasps this meaning; therefore, it points to a single thought-moment as the essential point for the practice of the phenomenal and the principle.

If one grasps this meaning, then the path of object and contemplation (*jìngguān*) of this school can be undertaken and practiced. There is no gateway for entering the Way or path for returning to the source that does not proceed by means of this.
If one were to cast aside deluded thoughts and seek a separate route of meaning elsewhere, how would this differ from discarding ice [to find water]?

"Seeking water, when will sentient beings attain Buddhahood? From this, it is known that those who do not follow the teachings of the Four Clarities (Sishiming) fail to grasp the essential intent of Tiantai;
failing to grasp the essential intent of Tiantai, they do not penetrate the meaning of the sutras and treatises.
Consequently, the words "for the sake of sentient beings" become utterly useless. As the ancients said: "To err by a hair's breadth is to lose one's way by a thousand li. This is indeed so.
A Warning. Xiu Xing of Biling said:
"When explaining principle, one eliminates all gradations; when discussing practice, one must accumulate merit before reaching the goal. This clarifies...

Regarding the doctrine of cultivation (*bhāvanā*) and nature (*prakṛti*): without cultivation, nature is not manifested; without nature, cultivation cannot be established. Therefore, the path of cultivation and nature must be clearly understood.
Generally, the dharma-gates discussed in the sūtras and śāstras do not transcend these two. It is not that there are no two dharmas;

rather, had the Buddha not appeared in the world, the meaning would have remained incomplete. Thus it is said: "Although nature is originally so, one relies on wisdom to initiate cultivation; through cultivation, one illuminates nature. Through [cultivation]...
Regarding the cultivation arising from the nature (*prakṛti*): if one discusses it according to the nature, then sentient beings and Buddhas are fundamentally without high or low;
how could there be any distinction between the primary and secondary, or between form and mind? It may be said that the *dharmadhātu* is equal, and delusion and awakening share the same path;

sentient beings are originally Buddhas. Regarding the nature, there is nothing for the Buddhas to speak of. Nevertheless, this is not the case when contrasted with cultivation. How could there be a "spontaneous Śākyamuni"?
The natural Maitreya does not rely on cultivation; yet, by what means can the secret treasury of the three virtues be realized?

Therefore, there exist the differences between the causes and effects of ordinary beings and sages, as well as the distinctions between self and other, high and low. Nevertheless, though they are different, they are essentially two yet non-dual.

Though they are non-dual, it does not hinder their being non-dual yet dual. According to the fundamental nature (*dharmatā*), the entirety of cultivation is present within the nature itself. As for its arising...
When one cultivates, the nature is fully realized as cultivation; cultivation and nature are identical, having no separate essence.

Although ordinary beings and sages are distinguished by high and low, the distinction between high and low is obliterated. Although delusion and awakening follow the same path, the difference between delusion and awakening remains intact.
Because True Suchness does not cling to its own nature, we know that the nature is fully realized as cultivation; because True Suchness does not lose its own substance, it is fully cultivation.
This is the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*). Therefore, the Way of the cultivated nature (*bhāvanā-svabhāva*) cannot be discussed [without reference to this].

Those who do not understand this, upon hearing that "the mind itself is Buddha," immediately abandon cultivation; or, upon hearing that the Buddha-way is long and distant, they consider themselves already devoid of the capacity for it.

All of this arises from failing to comprehend the teaching of the cultivated and perfected natures. Thus, we know that what is elucidated in the sūtras and śāstras does not go beyond these two. One who can understand this...
Such a person may be discussed with regarding the Way.
This concludes the "Eye of the Complete and Sudden School."
